checkpoints: Root cause: Secrets Manager bills per secret (~$0.40/secret/month) regardless of whether rotation is enabled, so with 40 secrets the team pays that charge 40 times a month for a rotation feature (4-step Lambda) they never actually use.

Recommended fix: migrate these 40 static config values to SSM Parameter Store SecureString — it still encrypts with KMS (same security level as Secrets Manager, no downgrade) but is entirely free at the standard tier, with no per-secret monthly charge.

Decision rule between the two services: Secrets Manager is worth its cost only when a secret needs scheduled automatic rotation (built-in 4-step rotation Lambda — createSecret/setSecret/testSecret/finishSecret — plus versioning staging labels for zero-downtime rollover, e.g. DB credentials or compliance-mandated API key rotation); for static/rarely-changing config like these 40 values, Parameter Store SecureString is sufficient.

Before migrating, confirm the 40 values don't hit Parameter Store's limitations: 4KB max size at standard tier (8KB with advanced tier at extra cost), no AWSCURRENT/AWSPREVIOUS versioning staging labels, and no cross-account sharing support.

Migration execution (parallel phase): keep the KMS encryption mechanism intact (no security downgrade) and create the corresponding values in SSM Parameter Store in parallel, running both stores side by side before cutover.
Update access control: change the reading service's IAM permission from secretsmanager:GetSecretValue to ssm:GetParameter (with WithDecryption = true) so it can read from the new source.
Cutover safely: test that the actual service successfully reads from the new source, then delete the old Secrets Manager secret afterward to stop paying for both simultaneously.

Defines `aws_organizations_policy` with `type = "SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY"` and JSON content containing a single `Effect = "Deny"` statement whose `Action` list includes all three actions (`organizations:LeaveOrganization`, `cloudtrail:StopLogging`, `cloudtrail:DeleteTrail`) with `Resource = "*"`.

Defines `aws_organizations_policy_attachment` that attaches the policy with `target_id` set to the OU itself (not the org root, not a single account), matching the "every account in that OU" requirement.
Identifies this as the deny-list strategy: leaves the default `FullAWSAccess` SCP (auto-attached by AWS to every org node) untouched, only adding the one targeted Deny statement.

Explains the advantage of deny-list over allow-list: no need to enumerate every allowed service (which risks implicit denial when AWS launches new services), only the already-known dangerous actions need to be blocked.

Explains why SCP is the correct layer instead of a regular IAM policy: an SCP binds the root user of every member account within its attachment scope, whereas an IAM policy only binds the specific identity it's attached to and can never restrict root.

Notes the prerequisite that the organization must have `feature_set = ALL` (not `CONSOLIDATED_BILLING`) and `enabled_policy_types = ["SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY"]` enabled on the org's root resource, otherwise `apply` fails with `PolicyTypeNotEnabledException`.
Three layers operate at three different SCOPES and solve three independent problems — they are not redundant; the final effective permission is always the INTERSECTION of all three layers.
SCP lives at the ORGANIZATION level (attached to root/OU/account within AWS Organizations) and binds EVERY principal in scope, INCLUDING the root user of a member account.
Permissions Boundary lives at the ACCOUNT level, attached to a SPECIFIC IAM user/role via the `permissions_boundary` argument, and does NOT bind root.

IAM policy attaches directly to an identity or resource and is the ONLY layer that actually GRANTS permission — SCP and Permissions Boundary only FILTER/set a ceiling, neither grants anything on its own.

Can't drop Permissions Boundary: SCP applies UNIFORMLY to an entire account or OU and can't be customized per-developer within the same account (e.g. restricting dev A to one region while dev B can use all regions) — Permissions Boundary exists precisely to give each identity a personalized ceiling when delegating self-service IAM creation.

Can't drop SCP: Permissions Boundary has no effect on the root user, so if a root access key leaks, the boundary does nothing — only SCP, which also binds root, remains an effective defense in that scenario.

Can't drop IAM policy: even if SCP and boundary both allow an action, without an explicit IAM policy granting it the request is still implicit-denied — permission only exists when an explicit IAM allow is present, while SCP/boundary merely decide whether that allow is permitted to pass through.
DO has exactly three access-control surfaces, no more.
PAT scope is a binary choice — read-only or full-access — decided once at token creation and stored in the DIGITALOCEAN_TOKEN env var.
PAT is not a Terraform resource, so its scope can't be reviewed or audited through a Terraform PR.
Spaces key grant is the real least-privilege surface for object storage: each key carries one or more {bucket, permission} pairs (read/readwrite/fullaccess), fully separate from the PAT.
Project is just an administrative grouping of resources by environment/billing with no permission field — placing a bucket in a "Production" project does not tighten access on it.
Compared to AWS IAM, DO lacks assume-role/STS, instance profiles, workload-identity federation, permission boundaries, org SCPs, per-action policies with condition keys, and a dedicated KMS.
Trade-off: fewer knobs means fewer places to get wrong (IAM misconfig is AWS's #1 vulnerability source), but also fewer defensive layers.
Practically, protecting access control on DO is mostly about protecting and rotating the right token/key, not writing policy.
Không đồng ý với đề xuất dùng `fullaccess` của đồng nghiệp.
Giải thích theo schema của DO: `fullaccess` yêu cầu `bucket` là chuỗi rỗng, nghĩa là key có quyền trên toàn bộ Spaces của account chứ không giới hạn vào 1 bucket cụ thể.
Chỉ ra hệ quả bảo mật: nếu key over-privileged này bị lộ, kẻ tấn công có thể write/delete trên MỌI bucket chứ không chỉ `reports`.
Đưa ra cách làm đúng: tạo Spaces key với đúng một grant block `{bucket = "reports", permission = "read"}`.
Nêu `permission` chỉ có 3 giá trị hợp lệ: `read`/`readwrite`/`fullaccess`.
Áp dụng nguyên tắc least privilege: luôn chọn giá trị permission thấp nhất vừa đủ cho nhu cầu (ở đây là `read`).
Nêu mỗi key có cặp access_key/secret_key riêng, nên thu hồi quyền của worker này chỉ cần xoá đúng key đó mà không ảnh hưởng các key khác — khác với việc sửa policy JSON dùng chung như ở IAM.
Đề xuất bước verify: thử PUT bằng key đó vào bucket, kỳ vọng trả về `AccessDenied` vì key chỉ có quyền read.
Disagrees with the teammate's reasoning — moving the bucket into the Production project does not make it safer or tighten access.
A DigitalOcean project (`digitalocean_project`) is purely an organizational/billing/audit grouping construct with no permission field whatsoever.
A project only carries descriptive metadata — `name`, `purpose`, and `environment` (restricted to Development/Staging/Production) — nothing related to access control.
Placing the bucket in the Production project doesn't restrict access: a `fullaccess` Spaces key or a write-scoped PAT can still write/delete on the bucket regardless of which project it's in.

This is unlike AWS Organizations with SCPs (a real org-level boundary that can block actions) or Azure's resource-group-as-scope — DigitalOcean has no equivalent access-control mechanism at the project layer.
To actually tighten access, review the Spaces key in use and switch its grant from `fullaccess` to `read`/`readwrite` scoped to the exact bucket needed.
Also review which PAT's scope currently has write/delete rights that could touch this resource.
`digitalocean_project_resources` separates attaching a resource URN from defining the project itself, further confirming a project is just a grouping layer, not a security boundary.
Root-cause diagnosis: both app-prod and db-staging carry the same VPC UUID — they are both sitting in the region's shared default VPC, visible directly in the doctl/terraform output.

Why it happened: app_prod's Terraform code never declares vpc_uuid, and per the Registry, leaving vpc_uuid empty makes the Droplet fall into the region's default VPC automatically — not "no VPC at all".

Not a firewall bug, and blast radius is region-wide: DO's Cloud Firewall only blocks traffic per rule/public exposure — it enforces no route tables or peering between Droplets sharing a VPC, so any Droplet in that region that also skips vpc_uuid (including another team's) lands in the same default VPC and can see each other's private IPs over eth1.
Verification step: run `doctl compute vpcs list` to confirm the exact default VPC pooling both Droplets.
Fix — isolate: create a dedicated custom `digitalocean_vpc` for the prod environment using a non-overlapping CIDR, e.g. `10.20.0.0/24`.
Fix — apply: add `vpc_uuid = digitalocean_vpc.prod.id` to app_prod and run `terraform apply`.
Fix — caveat: since `vpc_uuid` can't be updated in place, applying this change will destroy and recreate the app_prod Droplet.
Prevention going forward: every production Droplet must declare vpc_uuid explicitly and never fall back to the shared default VPC.

Security issue (most severe): the SSH rule (`port_range = "22"`) is open to `source_addresses = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]`, meaning every IP on the internet can SSH in — a classic anti-pattern ripe for brute-forcing
Fix for the security issue: narrow SSH access to a specific admin CIDR (or route it through a bastion/VPN) instead of leaving it open to the world
Design issue: the firewall is attached via `droplet_ids` hardcoding two specific Droplets, which doesn't fit a web server pool that scales up and down with load
Consequence of the design issue: every scale event requires editing the Terraform file and re-applying, easily leaving newly created Droplets unprotected

Fix for the design issue: attach the firewall by `tags` (e.g. `tags = [digitalocean_tag.web.id]`) instead of `droplet_ids`, so any Droplet carrying that tag is automatically covered, decoupling the rule from each Droplet's individual lifecycle

Relevant platform limits: a firewall attached by `droplet_ids` caps at 10 Droplets, while attaching by `tags` caps at 5 tags but each tag can group unlimited Droplets — a scaling pool should use tags to avoid hitting the 10-Droplet ceiling
Verification step: run `doctl compute firewall get` to confirm `Tags` is correct and the SSH rule no longer allows `0.0.0.0/0`
Verification step: attempt SSH from an IP outside the allowed range to confirm it is rejected

Identifies the root cause: the bucket-project association is declared in two places at once — directly inside `digitalocean_project`'s `resources` block, and again via a standalone `digitalocean_project_resources` resource — so both resources believe they own that association.

Explains the observed symptom follows from this double-ownership: on every `plan` Terraform sees one resource's applied state and the other resource trying to correct it back, producing an oscillating attach/detach even though nothing was actually changed.

States the intended purpose of `digitalocean_project_resources`: it exists to attach a Terraform-managed resource into a project that may be managed elsewhere (decoupling grouping from project definition), not to be used alongside a direct `resources` declaration on the same project.
Gives fix option A: when multiple teams/modules attach resources into a shared project, drop the `resources` attribute from `digitalocean_project` and keep only `digitalocean_project_resources`.

Gives fix option B: when a single module owns the whole project and its resources, keep `resources` directly in `digitalocean_project` and delete the `digitalocean_project_resources` resource entirely.

Describes the verification step: run `terraform plan` twice in a row with nothing changed; the second run must report `No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration`, otherwise some other place is still contesting URN ownership.

HCL answer: a `digitalocean_reserved_ip` resource (with `region`) plus a separate `digitalocean_reserved_ip_assignment` resource whose `ip_address` references the reserved IP and whose `droplet_id` points at `digitalocean_droplet.primary.id`.
A Reserved IP is a fixed public IPv4 — allocated once and never changing throughout its lifetime, regardless of which Droplet it's attached to.
Core design point: don't set `droplet_id` directly on `digitalocean_reserved_ip`; use a separate `digitalocean_reserved_ip_assignment` resource instead.
Per the Registry, the two assignment methods (inline on `reserved_ip` vs. via `reserved_ip_assignment`) cannot be used together — combining them causes state contention.

Why separate: failover becomes a one-line change — flipping `droplet_id` from `digitalocean_droplet.primary.id` to `digitalocean_droplet.secondary.id` and running `terraform apply` — which updates only the assignment resource; had `droplet_id` been set directly on `reserved_ip`, certain changes could instead force Terraform to recreate the IP itself, issuing a new address and breaking the "IP never changes, DNS doesn't need to know" goal.
Verify failover with `doctl compute reserved-ip get <ip> --format IP,DropletID` run before and after the change, confirming `IP` stays identical while `DropletID` switches from primary to secondary.
Avoid `terraform apply -replace` on the assignment resource, since that's a destroy-then-create (causing an outage), not the smooth re-assign mechanism DigitalOcean provides.
